statement: In adults with alcohol dependence at 11 US academic centres who had stopped drinking 4 to 21 days earlier (COMBINE, 1,383 people randomized, 2001 to 2004; Anton et al., 2006; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, with medicines and placebos donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, a maker of acamprosate, and several authors reporting fees or grants from drug companies), adding up to 20 sessions of a specialist talking therapy (combined behavioural intervention) to medicine or placebo pills and nine brief medical-support visits did not detectably change drinking during 16 weeks of treatment: averaged over the pill groups, abstinent days were 78.2 against 77.8 in 100 (Cohen d 0.01, 97.5% CI −0.12 to 0.14), an interval that excludes more than a small gain, while the chance of a first heavy-drinking day was not clearly lower (hazard ratio 0.81, 0.60 to 1.10, the paper's main-effect estimate, which by its interval may compare only the two groups on placebo pills), an interval that does not rule out a sizeable benefit. With naltrexone, the combination was no better than either alone: abstinent days were 77.1 in 100 with naltrexone and the therapy, 80.6 with naltrexone alone, 79.2 with the therapy and placebo pills and 75.1 with placebo pills alone (naltrexone × therapy interaction P = 0.009), and only naltrexone alone differed clearly from placebo pills alone (d 0.22, 0.03 to 0.40; therapy with placebo pills 0.17, −0.02 to 0.35; both 0.07, −0.11 to 0.25). More people had a good overall outcome at the end of treatment with naltrexone (74 in 100), the therapy (71) or both (74) than with placebo pills and medical support alone (58), a secondary outcome with more missing data than the main ones. People given the therapy without any pills or medical visits had fewer abstinent days (66.6 in 100) than those given placebo pills and medical support (73.8) or both (79.8). In the year after treatment the differences shrank and none was clear (abstinent days 61.4, 66.2, 66.6 and 67.3 in 100; interaction P = 0.27). The trial had low power for combinations (0.40 to 0.50), the therapy could not be hidden from participants, drinking was self-reported to staff who knew who had the therapy, and people needing psychiatric medicines or with other drug use disorders were left out. In most other trials of medicines both groups received some psychosocial treatment, so those trials show what medicines add to it (Jonas et al., 2014). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In one large US trial, adults with alcohol dependence who took naltrexone and had nine short check-ins with a health worker did as well as those who also had up to 20 sessions of specialist talking therapy: combining the two added nothing. On days without alcohol, only naltrexone without the therapy was clearly better than dummy pills; on an overall measure of doing well, naltrexone, the therapy or both were each better than dummy pills alone. People who had therapy without any pills or check-ins had fewer days without alcohol. A year after treatment the differences had mostly faded. The trial was not built to test combinations, and drinking was reported by the people themselves.
population: 1,383 adults with DSM-IV alcohol dependence, treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by advertisement and referral at 11 US academic sites, 4 to 21 days abstinent at entry, without other substance use disorders (except nicotine or cannabis) or psychiatric disorders requiring medication
exposure: A combined behavioural intervention (up to twenty 50-minute sessions with a specialist) added to medical management (nine visits with a health care professional) and naltrexone, acamprosate, both or placebo pills
comparator: The same pills and medical management without the therapy; for the no-pill group, placebo pills with medical management, with or without the therapy
outcome: Percent days abstinent and time to the first heavy drinking day during 16 weeks of treatment (coprimary); a composite good clinical outcome; the same measures in the year after treatment
magnitude: Anton et al. 2006 (COMBINE), during treatment: CBI main effect on percent days abstinent 78.2 against 77.8 (P=.82), Cohen d 0.01 (97.5% CI −0.12 to 0.14); time to first heavy drinking day HR 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10); naltrexone × CBI cells (pooled over acamprosate): placebo, no CBI 75.1; naltrexone, no CBI 80.6; CBI with placebo 79.2; naltrexone with CBI 77.1 (interaction P=.009); against placebo without CBI, d 0.22 (0.03 to 0.40), 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35) and 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25); good clinical outcome 58% (placebo, medical management), 74% (naltrexone), 71% (CBI with placebo), 74% (naltrexone with CBI), NNTs as printed 6, 7 and 7; CBI without pills or medical management 66.6 against 73.8 (placebo, medical management) and 79.8 (placebo, medical management and CBI). Year after treatment: 61.4, 66.2, 66.6 and 67.3 (interaction P=.27); CBI main effect 66.9 against 63.8 (P=.08). Power for interactions 0.40 to 0.50.

evidence.locator: Methods › Recruitment and Randomization, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and Assessment, 1st paragraph (p. 2004); Figure 1 (p. 2005); Treatment Conditions (p. 2006)
evidence.extracted: 1383 people with DSM-IV alcohol dependence, recruited by advertisements and clinical referrals at 11 US academic sites and abstinent for 4 to 21 days, were randomized to 9 groups: medical management (9 sessions with a health care professional) with naltrexone, acamprosate, both or two placebos, each with or without a combined behavioural intervention (CBI) delivered by specialists in up to twenty 50-minute sessions, or CBI alone without pills or medical management. People with other substance use disorders (except nicotine or cannabis) or psychiatric disorders requiring medication were excluded. The research assistants who assessed drinking were not blinded to psychosocial treatment.

evidence.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Drinking Outcomes for Pill-Taking Groups › Primary Outcomes, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 2009); Figure 2 (p. 2010)
evidence.extracted: Percent days abstinent during treatment, least-squares means: CBI 78.2 against no CBI 77.8 (P=.82); naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.009, with placebo and no CBI 75.1, naltrexone without CBI 80.6, CBI with placebo 79.2 and naltrexone with CBI 77.1 (pooled over acamprosate); the authors state that combined naltrexone and CBI showed no incremental benefit over CBI or naltrexone alone. Effect sizes (Cohen d, 97.5% CI): CBI main effect 0.01 (−0.12 to 0.14); against placebo naltrexone without CBI, naltrexone without CBI 0.22 (0.03 to 0.40), CBI without naltrexone 0.17 (−0.02 to 0.35), naltrexone with CBI 0.07 (−0.11 to 0.25). Time to the first heavy drinking day: CBI main-effect hazard ratio 0.81 (0.60 to 1.10); the paper does not say how its main-effect hazard ratios were coded, and by their intervals they may compare single groups rather than the whole factorial (a reporting issue on the study card).

Composite good clinical outcome over the last 8 weeks of treatment (abstinence, or moderate drinking without problems): naltrexone × CBI interaction P=.02; good outcome in 58% with placebo and medical management, 74% with naltrexone and medical management, 71% with placebo, CBI and medical management and 74% with naltrexone, CBI and medical management; numbers needed to treat 7 for CBI, 6 for naltrexone and 7 for both. Table 5 gives 1294 participants with data for this outcome; the study card notes that its cell percentages imply fewer.

evidence.locator: Results › Within-Treatment Evaluation of CBI Therapy Without Pills (Placebo Effect), 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2011, continuing on p. 2012); Table 5 (p. 2011)
evidence.extracted: Percent days abstinent during treatment: placebo pills and medical management 73.8, placebo pills with medical management and CBI 79.8, CBI alone without pills or medical management 66.6 (overall P<.001); corrected post hoc tests showed significant differences between the groups given pills and medical management and the group given CBI alone.

evidence.locator: Results › Posttreatment Follow-up Outcomes (p. 2012, continuing on p. 2013); Table 7 (p. 2013)
evidence.extracted: In the year after treatment the naltrexone × CBI interaction was no longer significant (P=.27): percent days abstinent 61.4 with placebo and medical management, 66.2 with naltrexone, 66.6 with CBI and 67.3 with naltrexone and CBI; CBI main effect 66.9 against 63.8 (P=.08).

Power was estimated above 0.90 for a main effect of each treatment on each coprimary end point and at 0.40 to 0.50 for an interaction half that size; the steering committee chose to ensure power for main effects and accept modest power for interactions.

evidence.locator: Financial Disclosures (p. 2015); Funding/Support and Role of the Sponsors (p. 2016)
evidence.extracted: Supported by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism; the acamprosate, naltrexone and matching placebos were donated by Lipha Pharmaceuticals, under whose Investigational New Drug application the study was conducted; Lipha monitored the sites and is stated to have had no role in data management, analysis, interpretation or the manuscript. Several authors report consultancy fees, honoraria or research support from drug companies.

Most included trials had psychosocial co-interventions, so the review's effect sizes reflect the added benefit of medication beyond psychosocial interventions and placebo; the largest trial, COMBINE, randomized 1383 treatment-seeking patients.

risk_of_bias.note: Study card sc_anton_2006 (RoB 2), overall some concerns: the therapy could not be blinded, drinking was self-reported to research assistants who knew who had the therapy, and the no-pill group was open by design; the medication contrasts themselves are at low risk.

indirectness.note: Worded for this trial's population and setting (US academic centres, recently abstinent treatment-seeking volunteers, both groups with medical management).

imprecision.note: Power for interactions 0.40 to 0.50; the hazard ratio for heavy drinking (0.81, 0.60 to 1.10) does not exclude a sizeable benefit; the contrast of the combination against naltrexone alone has no interval of its own.

publication_bias.note: Registered trial (NCT00006206) with all prespecified main effects and interactions reported.

grade.reasoning: A randomized trial starts high; rated down for risk of bias (unblinded therapy with self-reported outcomes) and imprecision (low power for combinations), giving low. 'Does not detectably change' rests on the main effect on abstinent days, whose interval excludes more than a small gain (d 0.14); the statement says that the heavy-drinking interval does not rule out a benefit and that the trial was not powered for combinations. Status single study. The other trials of medicines (Jonas et al., 2014) give both groups psychosocial treatment, so they do not test whether therapy adds to medicine and are cited only to frame what their estimates mean.
